spots.whyGo: The grubby door the slow horses trudge through in nearly every episode is a real one, on the corner of Aldersgate and Carthusian Street above an Italian restaurant - a genuinely unremarkable building doing a lot of work. The fire escape from the series is around the corner on St John's Street.
spots.opNote: A working office building above a restaurant - the point is the doorway and the street, both public. Two minutes from Barbican station and Smithfield.

spots.name: Snatch's Diamond Store
spots.subject: Snatch (2000) - Doug the Head's diamond store
spots.whyGo: Doug the Head's diamond shop in Snatch is on Hatton Garden, London's real diamond district - and his "local" in the film is Ye Olde Mitre, already on this site, a couple of doors down.
spots.opNote: A working commercial building on Hatton Garden - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Snatch's Pawn Shop
spots.subject: Snatch (2000) - Sol's pawn shop
spots.whyGo: One of several genuine East End addresses Guy Ritchie used in Snatch - an ordinary Bethnal Green street standing in for the criminal underworld of the film.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Snatch's Tailor (Bethnal Green Town Hall)
spots.subject: Snatch (2000) - Franky Four Fingers's tailor
spots.address: Cambridge Heath Road at Patriot Square
spots.whyGo: The historic 1910 town hall building - already on this site as the Town Hall Hotel - played the tailor's shop in Snatch. The film angle is a genuinely different reason to know this building beyond staying there.
spots.opNote: Now a hotel - see the Hotels section for how to book a stay.

spots.name: Somerset House
spots.subject: GoldenEye (1995) - the St Petersburg tank chase
spots.whyGo: Bond drives a tank through St Petersburg in a courtyard three minutes from Waterloo Bridge. The neoclassical facades were close enough to Russian imperial architecture to pass, so the production never left London.
spots.opNote: The courtyard is free and open daily - fountains in summer, an ice rink in winter. Exhibitions inside are ticketed.

spots.name: South Molton Street
spots.subject: Love Actually (2003) - the Christmas lights montage
spots.whyGo: The pedestrianised street used in the film's opening montage of London at Christmas. Narrow, Georgian and hung with lights every December, which is precisely why it was picked.
spots.opNote: Free, always open, pedestrian only. Two minutes from Bond Street. Worth timing for late November onwards when the lights go up.

spots.name: St Alphage Ruins & Salters' Garden
spots.subject: Medieval church ruins and a fragment of the Roman city wall, wedged between Barbican towers
spots.whyGo: A tiny public garden holds the ruins of St Alphage London Wall church alongside a real stretch of the Roman and medieval city wall, crenellated in 1477 - genuinely ancient London hiding in the concrete geometry of the Barbican.
spots.opNote: Free, always open, easy to walk straight past - it's set back from London Wall itself, reached via Fore Street.

spots.name: St Bartholomew the Great
spots.subject: Sherlock Holmes (2009) - the interior standing in for St Paul's
spots.whyGo: London's oldest surviving parish church, founded in 1123, its Norman interior standing in for St Paul's during the human-sacrifice scene. Four Weddings and Shakespeare in Love were shot here too - it is the most filmed church in the city.
spots.opNote: A working church with a small admission charge for visitors and free entry for worship. Closed to sightseers during services. Barbican or Farringdon, five minutes.

spots.name: St Bartholomew's Hospital
spots.subject: Sherlock (2010-2017) - the fall from the roof in The Reichenbach Fall
spots.whyGo: Sherlock jumps from the roof of the pathology block and lands on the pavement below. Fans left so many notes on the phone box and the wall outside that the hospital had to manage it. Barts is also the oldest hospital in Britain still on its original site, founded in 1123.
spots.opNote: A working hospital. The exterior and the square are public; the small museum keeps limited hours. Keep out of the way of patients.

spots.name: St George in the East
spots.subject: The Long Good Friday (1980) - the car bomb outside the church
spots.whyGo: Hawksmoor's 1729 church, where a bomb intended for Harold Shand nearly kills his mother. It was gutted in the Blitz and rebuilt with a modern church inside the surviving shell, which is why the interior is such a surprise.
spots.opNote: Free and normally open during the day, with a churchyard that functions as a public garden. Shadwell on the Overground or DLR, three minutes.

spots.name: St John's Square
spots.subject: Paddington 2 (2017) - the theatrical agent's office
spots.whyGo: The Clerkenwell square used for the office where Buchanan's agent delivers bad news. St John's Gate, the Tudor arch across the square, is the surviving gatehouse of a twelfth-century priory.
spots.opNote: Free, a public square, always open. The Museum of the Order of St John in the gatehouse is free and open Monday to Saturday. Farringdon, three minutes.

spots.name: St Katharine Docks
spots.subject: The Long Good Friday (1980) - Harold's yacht and the pier party
spots.whyGo: The marina where Bob Hoskins holds court on his yacht and pitches his vision of a redeveloped Docklands - a speech the film treats as hubris and history proved right. The basin was one of the first docks converted, in 1973.
spots.opNote: Free, open at all hours, ringed by pubs and restaurants keeping normal hours. Five minutes east of Tower Bridge, and Tower Hill is the nearest station.

spots.name: Stanley Gardens
spots.subject: Spectre (2015) - the exterior of Bond's own London flat
spots.whyGo: The stucco terrace used for where James Bond actually lives, which the films almost never show. Notting Hill rather than Chelsea or Mayfair, which surprised a lot of people at the time.
spots.opNote: A residential street - people live here. Free to walk down, always open, five minutes from Notting Hill Gate. Look, do not linger at doorways.

spots.name: Star Yard Victorian Urinal
spots.subject: A Grade II-listed 1851 cast-iron street urinal, one of the last of its kind
spots.whyGo: Manufactured in Glasgow in 1851, tucked down a narrow yard off Chancery Lane - one of only a handful of cast-iron pissoirs left in London, and the only one carrying a royal coat of arms. No longer in use, but still standing.
spots.opNote: Locked and non-functional, but visible from the street in Star Yard at any time.

spots.name: Stoney Street
spots.subject: Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (2004) - the Leaky Cauldron exterior
spots.whyGo: The third film moved the Leaky Cauldron here, to the brick railway arches on the edge of Borough Market - a completely different building from the Leadenhall Market version used in the first film. Both are canon and both are in London.
spots.opNote: Free and open, a public street through the market. Borough Market's own trading hours make the difference between atmospheric and deserted; London Bridge station is two minutes away.

spots.name: Sylvia Pankhurst's Chelsea Home
spots.subject: Sylvia Pankhurst (1882–1960), suffragette and campaigner
spots.whyGo: Pankhurst's plaque sits on the same riverside street as George Eliot's - two very different kinds of significance a few doors apart.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Sylvia Plath's Primrose Hill Home
spots.subject: Sylvia Plath (1932–1963), poet
spots.whyGo: Plath and Ted Hughes lived here early in their marriage - one of the more poignant plaques on the map, a short walk from Primrose Hill itself.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: T.S. Eliot's Kensington Home
spots.subject: T.S. Eliot (1888–1965), poet
spots.whyGo: Eliot lived here in his later years, having already written The Waste Land and Four Quartets - one of Kensington's several literary plaques.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Tabernacle Street
spots.subject: Love Actually (2003) - the office where Colin delivers sandwiches
spots.whyGo: The street used for the office where Colin makes his catering rounds and his hopeless attempts at flirtation. Shoreditch standing in for a generic London workplace, before Shoreditch became a look.
spots.opNote: Free, a public street, always open. Five minutes from Old Street or Moorgate.

spots.name: Talgarth Road
spots.subject: Trainspotting (1996) - Renton's London flat
spots.whyGo: The Art Deco block used for the flat Renton takes when he moves south, in the film's brief and unhappy London chapter. It is on the A4, one of the loudest roads in west London, which suits the scene.
spots.opNote: Residential, exterior only, free and always visible. Barons Court, three minutes. There is no reason to come for this alone.

spots.name: Tate Modern
spots.subject: Match Point (2005) - the gallery opening
spots.whyGo: The gallery where Chris runs into Nola again and the film turns. The Turbine Hall does a lot of work in British cinema as shorthand for the moneyed art world.
spots.opNote: Free entry to the collection, daily 10am to 6pm, with Level 10's free viewing bar open to 9pm on Fridays and Saturdays. Southwark or Blackfriars, or across the Millennium Bridge from St Paul's.

spots.name: Ted Lasso's Crown & Anchor (The Prince's Head)
spots.subject: Ted Lasso (2020-2023) - the team's local pub
spots.whyGo: The pub Ted and the Greyhounds fans drink in is The Prince's Head on Richmond Green, and the exterior is exactly as it appears on screen. Richmond doubles for itself throughout - unusually for London television, the show is set where it was shot.
spots.opNote: A working Fuller's pub, normal opening hours. The interior scenes were shot on a set, so do not expect the inside to match.

spots.name: Temple of Mithras (London Mithraeum)
spots.subject: A Roman temple, discovered in 1954, now beneath Bloomberg's HQ
spots.whyGo: Roman Londoners worshipped Mithras here around 240 AD; the ruins were rediscovered during 1954 building work and drew such crowds that the Prime Minister had to weigh in. Now sunk seven metres below Bloomberg's building, with a free reconstruction of temple worship - dimmed lights, chanting, atmospheric smoke.
spots.opNote: Free, but timed-entry tickets must be booked online in advance - it sells out, especially weekends. Closed Sundays and Mondays.

spots.name: Ten Trinity Square
spots.subject: Skyfall (2012) - M is summoned to meet the incoming Gareth Mallory
spots.whyGo: The Beaux-Arts former Port of London Authority headquarters, now a Four Seasons hotel, playing the establishment room where M gets told her time is up. The rotunda and the coffered ceiling are the shot, and they are still exactly as filmed.
spots.opNote: A working hotel, so the lobby and bars are open to non-residents. Two minutes from Tower Hill. Free to walk in and look; you are expected to buy something if you sit down.

spots.name: The (What's the Story) Morning Glory? Cover Site
spots.subject: Oasis, (What's the Story) Morning Glory? (1995) - the album cover street
spots.whyGo: Shot at dawn on a Sunday in July 1995, between the record shops that made Berwick Street the centre of London's vinyl trade. Sister Ray still trades on the street, which is more than most locations on this list can say.
spots.opNote: A public street, walkable any time. Best early on a Sunday if you want the empty-street look of the sleeve - the market stalls fill it on weekdays.

spots.name: The Abbey Road Crossing
spots.subject: The Beatles, Abbey Road (1969) - the album cover crossing
spots.address: Abbey Road at Grove End Road
spots.whyGo: The most photographed zebra crossing in the world, outside the studios where most of the Beatles' catalogue was recorded. The crossing itself is Grade II listed - the only pedestrian crossing in Britain that is.
spots.opNote: A LIVE ROAD with real traffic, and drivers here have seen the joke several thousand times. The studio is a working facility and is not open to the public; the wall outside is covered in graffiti and repainted regularly.

spots.name: The Amy Winehouse Statue
spots.subject: Amy Winehouse (1983-2011), in the market she lived beside and sang about
spots.whyGo: A life-size bronze by Scott Eaton, unveiled on 14 September 2014 - what would have been her 31st birthday - standing in the Stables Market a few minutes from where she lived. She is in the beehive and the winged eyeliner, with a Star of David at her throat, and the plinth carries the line 'Love is a losing game'.
spots.opNote: Free, outdoors and always accessible, in the Stables Market end of Camden rather than by the lock - walk north past the railway bridge. Fans leave flowers, notes and lipstick marks on it, particularly around her birthday in September and the anniversary of her death in July.

spots.name: The Beatles' Rooftop Concert (3 Savile Row)
spots.subject: The Beatles' final public performance, 30 January 1969
spots.whyGo: The Beatles played their last ever public set on this roof - a 42-minute performance from the top of their Apple Corps headquarters that stopped traffic on Savile Row until the police arrived and asked them to turn it down.
spots.opNote: The roof is not accessible and the building is in private commercial use - this is a look-up-from-the-pavement stop. A few doors from the Kingsman tailor at number 11.

spots.name: The British Museum
spots.subject: The Mummy Returns (2001) - the museum sequence
spots.whyGo: Filmed at the museum itself, though the exterior shots used UCL's front quad up the road because the real facade was behind scaffolding at the time. Two Bloomsbury buildings, one museum, in the same film.
spots.opNote: Free and open daily. Use the Montague Place entrance at the back to avoid the main queue.

spots.name: The Crown's Buckingham Palace (Old Royal Naval College)
spots.subject: The Crown (2016-2023) - the Buckingham Palace exterior and courtyard
spots.address: Old Royal Naval College, King William Walk
spots.whyGo: Wren's naval college stands in for Buckingham Palace throughout the series - the real palace does not allow filming, so the courtyard scenes you remember were shot in Greenwich. The same colonnades appear in Les Miserables, Thor and The Dark Knight Rises.
spots.opNote: The grounds are free and open daily; the Painted Hall and Chapel are ticketed separately. Already the most-filmed building in London, so expect to recognise it from several things at once.

spots.name: The Dark Knight Rises's Italian Cafe (Old Royal Naval College)
spots.subject: The Dark Knight Rises (2012) - Alfred spots Bruce and Selina
spots.whyGo: The riverside colonnades here stood in for a Florence street cafe in the film's final scene - a different Greenwich landmark angle from the Bridgerton connection already on this site.
spots.opNote: Free grounds, open daily; the buildings themselves have their own separate opening hours and some charge for entry.

spots.name: The Dublin Castle
spots.subject: The small back room where Madness, Blur and Amy Winehouse all played
spots.whyGo: A back room the size of a living room with a genuine claim on British music - Madness effectively started here, Blur played early sets, and Amy Winehouse both performed and worked behind the bar. Still a working music pub putting on new bands most nights.
spots.opNote: Free or a few pounds on the door depending on the night. Small enough that arriving late means standing in the corridor.

spots.name: The Ferryman's Seat
spots.subject: The last surviving stone perch used by Thames boatmen waiting for customers
spots.whyGo: Before bridges crossed this stretch of the Thames, watermen ferried Londoners across for a fee - this stone seat, set into a wall near the Globe, is the last of the perches they waited on. Genuinely easy to walk straight past.
spots.opNote: Set into a wall on a public street, visible any time, a couple of minutes from Shakespeare's Globe.

spots.name: The Floating Pocket Park
spots.subject: A small planted island moored in Paddington Basin
spots.whyGo: A genuinely floating garden moored in the basin, reached across the Rolling Bridge already on this site - trees, planting and benches on a platform that rises and falls with the water, which is not a sentence most London green spaces earn.
spots.opNote: Free, always accessible on foot from the towpath. Small - ten minutes is enough unless you plan to sit and stay.

spots.name: The Hawley Arms
spots.subject: Amy Winehouse's Camden local - she worked behind the bar and kept coming back
spots.whyGo: The Victorian pub just off the market where Amy Winehouse pulled pints - first as staff, later as a regular who would hop back behind the bar for the sake of it. She stayed loyal to it after fame arrived, drinking and playing pool here, and helped raise the money to reopen it after the February 2008 Camden Lock fire gutted the building.
spots.opNote: A working pub, not a shrine - it does not trade on her and there is no memorial inside. Also the 2000s haunt of Kate Moss, Noel Fielding and most of the indie scene. Her drink here was the 'Rickstasy': three parts vodka to one each of banana liqueur, Southern Comfort and Baileys.

spots.name: The Hempel Zen Garden
spots.subject: Notting Hill (1999) - William and Anna's wedding reception
spots.whyGo: The walled garden used for the wedding reception at the end of the film, in a hotel that was one of the first minimalist design hotels in London. It is a private garden square rather than a park.
spots.opNote: Part of a hotel - access depends on the hotel, not on the public. Free to see the square from the street. Ten minutes from Paddington or Lancaster Gate.

spots.name: The Imitation Game's MI6 (Lethaby Building)
spots.subject: The Imitation Game (2014) - MI6 headquarters interiors
spots.whyGo: A Central Saint Martins building doubled as MI6's wartime headquarters for Benedict Cumberbatch's Alan Turing to walk through - a working art-school building most passersby would never connect to the film.
spots.opNote: A working educational building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: The Jerusalem Tavern
spots.subject: Judy (2019) - Judy and Mickey stop for a drink
spots.whyGo: A single-room eighteenth-century shopfront pub, the London tap for St Peter's Brewery, used for a quiet scene between Garland and her last husband. It seats about thirty people and looks two hundred years older than it is licensed to be.
spots.opNote: A working pub, normal hours, and often full by six on a weekday. Free to walk into. Farringdon, four minutes.

spots.name: The King's Cross Light Tunnel
spots.subject: A permanently colour-lit pedestrian subway between the stations and Granary Square
spots.whyGo: An ordinary underpass connecting the stations to Granary Square, lit end to end in shifting colour - free, always open, and one of the most photographed short walks in the area precisely because almost nobody expects a subway to look like this.
spots.opNote: Open to pedestrians 7am-8pm daily. Takes about two minutes to walk; most of what there is to see, you see from either end.

spots.name: The Millennium Bridge
spots.subject: Harry Potter and the Half-Blood Prince (2009) - Death Eaters destroy the bridge
spots.whyGo: Collapsed into the Thames in the opening minutes of the sixth film. In reality it is the pedestrian bridge from St Paul's to Tate Modern, and the walk across it gives the best straight-on view of the cathedral in London.
spots.opNote: Free, open at all times, busiest at weekends. Two minutes from Tate Modern.

spots.name: The National Gallery
spots.subject: Skyfall (2012) - Bond meets Q in front of The Fighting Temeraire
spots.whyGo: Bond and Q sit on a bench in front of Turner's painting of a warship being towed away to be broken up, and the scene makes its point about obsolescence without anybody having to say it. The painting is on permanent display and free to see.
spots.opNote: Free and open daily, with one late evening a week. Ask at the desk for the Turner rooms - they get asked constantly.

spots.name: The Old Curiosity Shop
spots.subject: Likely London's oldest surviving shop building, dating to around 1567
spots.whyGo: A crooked, half-timbered survivor from the 1560s, built from salvaged ship timber - it outlasted the Great Fire and the Blitz. Long claimed (without firm evidence) as the inspiration for Dickens's novel of the same name.
spots.opNote: A shopfront on a public street, viewable any time; now owned by LSE.

spots.name: The Old Royal Naval College
spots.subject: Thor: The Dark World (2013) - the Greenwich finale
spots.whyGo: Thor and Malekith fight through the colonnades in the film's climax, and Greenwich plays itself rather than standing in for anywhere. Wren's buildings have doubled for Paris, St Petersburg and Gotham in other productions.
spots.opNote: The grounds are free and open daily. The Painted Hall is ticketed and worth it on its own terms.

spots.name: The Pankhursts' Notting Hill Home
spots.subject: Emmeline and Christabel Pankhurst, suffragette leaders
spots.whyGo: A mother-and-daughter plaque for two of the central figures of the British suffragette movement, on a residential street off Holland Park Avenue.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: The Royal Oak
spots.subject: The Krays (1990) - the pub gets smashed up
spots.whyGo: The corner pub wrecked in the film's turf-war scene, on the street that fills with the flower market every Sunday. The exterior is largely unchanged.
spots.opNote: A working pub with normal opening hours. Columbia Road Flower Market runs Sunday mornings only, roughly 8am to 3pm, and the street is impassable while it does. Hoxton is the nearest station.

spots.name: The Salisbury Hotel
spots.subject: The Long Good Friday (1980) - Fagan's, the Irish pub
spots.whyGo: An extravagantly ornate 1899 gin palace standing in for a fictional Irish pub. Etched glass, mahogany and a ceiling that has no business being in a suburban pub - it is Grade II* listed and largely intact.
spots.opNote: A working pub with normal hours, free to walk into. Manor House on the Piccadilly line, five minutes, then a walk up Green Lanes.

spots.name: The Seven Noses of Soho
spots.subject: Sculpted noses glued to buildings in 1997, a protest against rising CCTV surveillance
spots.address: Multiple sites, incl. Admiralty Arch and Meard Street
spots.whyGo: Artist Rick Buckley cast his own nose in plaster and stuck copies on buildings across central London in 1997, protesting the spread of CCTV. Most were removed; seven are said to survive, and a rumour promises riches to anyone who finds all of them.
spots.opNote: Free, on public building exteriors, findable any time - no official map, part of the appeal is the hunt.

spots.name: The Shard
spots.subject: Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019) - Fury and Hill watch the drone attack
spots.whyGo: Where Nick Fury and Maria Hill watch London come apart from a great height. The building has appeared in more London-under-attack sequences than any other since it topped out in 2012.
spots.opNote: The View from The Shard occupies floors 68 to 72, including an open-air deck; hours change by date so check the calendar. Aqua Shard on level 31 has no admission fee if you book a table. London Bridge station is underneath.

spots.name: The Treasury Building, Great George Street
spots.subject: Spectre (2015) - the government exteriors
spots.whyGo: The Edwardian government block off Whitehall stands in for the security establishment Bond spends the film fighting. The Churchill War Rooms sit underneath the same building.
spots.opNote: Viewable from the street; the building is not open to the public. The War Rooms below are ticketed and need booking ahead.

spots.name: The Wannabe Staircase (St Pancras Renaissance)
spots.subject: Spice Girls, Wannabe (1996) - the video's grand staircase
spots.address: St Pancras Renaissance Hotel, Euston Road
spots.whyGo: The single-take video that launched the band was shot on George Gilbert Scott's Grand Staircase and through the lobby here. It was only filmed in London by accident - the shoot was booked for a building in Barcelona and the permissions fell through days before.
spots.opNote: A WORKING HOTEL, and the staircase is not a public thoroughfare - it is reachable if you are staying or eating at the Booking Office bar, otherwise ask at reception rather than wandering in. The station side is public and free.

spots.name: The Whispering Gallery, St Paul's
spots.subject: Paddington 2 (2017) - the search for the pop-up book clue
spots.whyGo: The circular gallery inside the dome where a whisper against the wall carries round to the far side, used as Buchanan hunts for the next clue. It is 257 steps up, the first of the three galleries.
spots.opNote: Included in the £27 adult sightseeing ticket, which also covers the Stone and Golden Galleries at 376 and 528 steps. Stairs only, no lift. Monday to Saturday, last entry around 4pm. St Paul's station.

spots.name: The Ziggy Stardust Cover Site
spots.subject: David Bowie, The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars (1972)
spots.whyGo: Bowie posed under a streetlamp here on a wet January night in 1972 for the Ziggy Stardust sleeve. The K. West furrier's sign behind him is long gone, but a black plaque marks the exact spot - black rather than blue because the Crown Estate put it up, not English Heritage.
spots.opNote: Free, on a pedestrianised street now full of restaurant tables. The plaque is at pavement level and easy to walk straight past.

spots.name: Throgmorton Avenue
spots.subject: Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation (2015) - Solomon Lane goes through a window
spots.whyGo: The gated City lane where the villain confronts Hunt and exits through plate glass. It is a private road with iron gates at both ends, which is why it looks so unlike a normal street.
spots.opNote: Free to walk through on weekdays; the gates are closed at night and at weekends, which catches people out. Two minutes from Bank or Moorgate.

spots.name: Tower Bridge, West Upper Walkway
spots.subject: Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019) - the battle for the bridge
spots.whyGo: The high-level walkway where the film's climax plays out, glass floor and all. It is the same walkway you can stand on with an £18 ticket, which makes this one of the few blockbuster finales you can literally visit.
spots.opNote: The Exhibition is £18 adult, daily 9.30am to 6pm with last entry at 5pm, and there is lift access to the walkways. The bridge itself and its pavements are free at all hours. Tower Hill, two minutes.

spots.name: Tower of London
spots.subject: Spider-Man: Far From Home (2019) - the school trip arrives
spots.whyGo: The visitors' entrance where Happy Hogan delivers the school party, on the London leg of the film's European tour. The Tower gets destroyed later, which the guidebooks tend to leave out.
spots.opNote: Ticketed and expensive, and busiest between 11am and 3pm. The moat, the wharf and the view of the White Tower from the free pavement cost nothing. Tower Hill, two minutes.

spots.name: Trafalgar Square
spots.subject: Wonder Woman (2017) - the Armistice celebrations
spots.whyGo: Dressed as 1918 London for the film's closing celebration. The square has appeared as itself in more productions than almost anywhere else in the city.
spots.opNote: Free and open at all times. The National Gallery on the north side is also free.

spots.name: Trafalgar Square's "Smallest Police Station"
spots.subject: A hollowed-out lamppost built as a covert police observation post in 1926
spots.whyGo: Tucked into the square's southeast corner, this booth was built in 1926 from a hollowed-out ornamental lamppost so up to two officers could quietly watch the square during demonstrations. It's often billed as "Britain's smallest police station", though it never technically had that status.
spots.opNote: Free, visible from the street, easy to miss entirely if you don't know to look for it - it looks like a lamppost.

spots.name: Trinity Buoy Wharf
spots.subject: London's only lighthouse, a shipping-container art village, and a Victorian steamship museum
spots.whyGo: A genuinely odd little peninsula at the mouth of the Lea: London's only lighthouse (used to test navigation lights, not to guide ships), a village of creative studios built from shipping containers, and the SS Robin, a preserved 1890 steamship.
spots.opNote: Free to walk around; the lighthouse's Longplayer sound installation is open weekend afternoons. It is NOT next to Canary Wharf - allow 20-30 minutes on foot from the Wharf, or take the DLR to East India and walk about 10 minutes. Nothing on the Jubilee line goes near it.

spots.name: Virginia and Leonard Woolf's Richmond Home
spots.subject: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941) and Leonard Woolf, at Hogarth House
spots.whyGo: The Woolfs lived here 1915-1924 and founded the Hogarth Press on the premises, printing early editions of Woolf's own novels and T.S. Eliot's poetry on a hand press in the house.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only. See also the earlier Woolf plaque in Fitzrovia.

spots.name: Virginia Woolf's Fitzroy Square Home
spots.subject: Virginia Woolf (1882–1941), writer, publisher and literary critic
spots.whyGo: Woolf lived here 1907-1911, in the Bloomsbury Group's earliest years before the name Bloomsbury attached itself to the circle. She has a second plaque in Richmond from her later years.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only. See also the Richmond plaque at Hogarth House.

spots.name: Where Keith Moon Played
spots.subject: Keith Moon (1946–1978), drummer, The Who
spots.whyGo: Marks where The Who played in the earliest days of the band, rather than a home address - a different kind of plaque story from the usual "lived here".
spots.opNote: On the former Marquee Club site, now a different business - the plaque is the only trace of the venue at street level.

spots.name: Where Television Was Born
spots.subject: John Logie Baird (1888–1946), television pioneer
spots.whyGo: Baird gave the first public demonstration of television in an attic room here in 1926 - a genuinely world-changing moment on an ordinary Soho street.
spots.opNote: The building is now Bar Italia at street level; the plaque is above.

spots.name: Wilcox Road
spots.subject: My Beautiful Laundrette (1985) - Powders, the launderette
spots.whyGo: The street where Omar and Johnny do up the launderette, in the film that made Daniel Day-Lewis's name and put a gay interracial relationship on British screens in 1985. The shopfront was dressed for the film and is an ordinary parade again.
spots.opNote: A residential street, free and open. Wandsworth Road station, or Stockwell on the Northern and Victoria lines, ten minutes.

spots.name: Wilkie Collins's Home
spots.subject: Wilkie Collins (1824–1889), novelist
spots.whyGo: Collins wrote here as one of the pioneers of the detective novel - The Moonstone and The Woman in White both date from his years on this street.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: William Morris's Red Lion Square Home
spots.subject: William Morris (1834–1896), designer and decorative artist
spots.whyGo: Morris founded his decorative arts firm from this address in 1861, before the patterns that now cover half of Britain's National Trust properties existed.
spots.opNote: A private/commercial building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Wilton's Music Hall
spots.subject: The Krays (1990) - the interior of the twins' nightclub
spots.whyGo: The oldest surviving grand music hall in the world, built in 1859 behind a row of terraced houses, used as the interior of the Krays' club. It has been deliberately conserved rather than restored, so the peeling paint is the point.
spots.opNote: A working theatre and bar. The Mahogany Bar is free to walk into and open most evenings; the auditorium depends on the programme. Tower Hill or Shadwell, five minutes.

spots.name: Winchester Palace Ruins
spots.subject: The Great Hall wall and rose window of a medieval bishop's palace
spots.whyGo: One wall of the Bishop of Winchester's Great Hall, rose window still intact, standing on an ordinary pavement between the Golden Hinde and the Clink Prison Museum - surrounded now by Borough Market's restaurant crowds rather than the medieval palace it was once part of. Surfaced in research months ago and never actually written up until now.
spots.opNote: Free, viewable from the street at any time. A small medieval-style garden sits inside the ruin, planted by the Bankside Open Spaces Trust.

spots.name: Winston Churchill's Last Home
spots.subject: Winston Churchill (1874–1965), Prime Minister
spots.whyGo: Churchill's home for the last years of his life, a short walk from the Kensington museums.
spots.opNote: A private residential building - viewable from the street only.

spots.name: Ye Olde Mitre
spots.subject: A pub built in 1546 down an alley with no street sign
spots.whyGo: Founded in 1546 for the Bishop of Ely's household staff, tucked down a narrow passage off Hatton Garden with nothing marking the entrance - most people who work nearby never find it. A preserved cherry tree trunk inside is said to mark where Elizabeth I danced with Sir Christopher Hatton.
spots.opNote: No sign on the street - look for the narrow gap between the buildings on Hatton Garden opposite number 8. Two tiny wood-panelled rooms, low ceilings, gets busy after work.
